passage:
The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson on her first visit to the shed. Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish it in his yard, and Grandfather had laughed.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather ran his thumb along the break, went to the telephone, and told Mr. Corran that a yard which sold green cedar to an old friend ought to be ashamed. He wanted a fresh board by Friday.

I spent the afternoon checking. My times at the steam box matched the ones he had taught me, and his measuring agreed with the plans to the sixteenth. I kept coming back to the window. The split plank was the only one the sun reached after noon, when the tin roof held the heat like an oven, and its twin on the shaded side, cut from the same cedar board, was as sound as the day I bent it.

“Well, Ada,” Grandfather said when I showed him, and stood at the window a long time. The next morning was fair and still, and he spent it tacking canvas over the glass and fitting a new plank. That evening Mrs. Vale came to ask whether her grandson could sail the Linnet in the regatta. I had hoped Grandfather would keep it for us, or set it aside to be rebuilt next summer, but he told her it was hers once the repair was done.

On regatta day I stood on the seawall while her grandson took the Linnet out past the moorings. I knew every plank in her, which ones I had bent and which he had, and I followed the white sail until it went behind the point, and for a while after that.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish the boat in his yard, and Grandfather had laughed.

Grandfather told her to come back when the hull was closed. After she left he said she had a good eye, and he whistled through the rest of the day.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather looked at it, then at me. “How long was it in the box, Ada?” For the rest of that week he did the steaming himself, standing over the box in the heat with his watch in his hand, and he began to talk of setting the boat aside to be rebuilt next summer.

On Saturday I took the plans down to look at the fourth station. In the margin, in his father’s hand, was a note: too sharp here, eased on the first Linnet. We measured the frames again, and they matched the drawing exactly. He eased the curve where his father had eased it and repaired the plank, and when Mrs. Vale offered a fair price that evening, he told her the Linnet was spoken for. I would sail it in the regatta.

I sailed it in his old cap and came in fifth. That night I swept the shed, oiled his tools and hung them back in their places, and under his father’s note, in my smallest letters, I wrote the date and four words: he gave me this.

Grandfather rowed across, and by noon Mr. Corran’s men were towing the Linnet over to be repaired and finished in his yard, with a fair wind behind them.

I stayed in the shed. The man who had sold us wet cedar would put his own brass plate on her transom, and at the regatta people would say what a fine boat Corran’s yard had built. Grandfather said he would think it over, which in our family can mean anything.

I showed him the page. He read it twice. Then he said a repaired plank in a hurried hull would split again in the first heat of August, and that next summer the two of us would rebuild the Linnet properly. The regatta would have to manage without her.

Mrs. Vale found another boat for her grandson, and Grandfather says next summer the way other people say tomorrow. I watched him fumble the latch on the shed door that night, three tries before it caught, and in my room I counted the months to June, and then counted them again.

passage:
The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson to sail on her first visit to the shed. Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish it in his yard, and Grandfather had laughed.

The plans hung above the bench. His father drew them one winter at the kitchen table, with a ruler cut from a broken oar, and every Linnet since had come from those sheets. The margins were crowded with notes in two hands, his father’s upright and his own leaning, and he touched them in passing, the way people touch a doorframe.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather took the plans down and spread them on the bench. “He always drew her too sharp in the bow, Ada,” he said, and for two days, in the heat of the shed, he went over his father’s lines with a magnifying glass. I asked whether we should set the boat aside to be rebuilt next summer, and he kept reading.

On the third day I held the tape while he measured the frames again. At the fourth station his own pencil mark sat a quarter inch from the line on the drawing. He looked at it a while, rolled the plans up, and repaired the plank that afternoon. When Mrs. Vale asked again to buy it, he said he would race the Linnet himself. He had been a fair sailor once, and he meant to find out whether he still was.

On regatta day he took her out with his stiff hands taped and handled the tiller like a young man. He came in sixth of eleven. I watched every tack from the seawall, and that winter I practiced his bowline until I could tie it the way he does, with my eyes closed.

For thirty-two years Ezra Holm kept the light on Gannet Point, the low headland guarding the channel into Kelby. Off the point lie the breakers of Tarrow Shoal; Kelby's harbor lamp burned two miles farther up, and on clear nights both lights were visible from the gallery. In fog a bell was rung by hand for every vessel that passed inside the point, and his daughter Lise kept the logbook. Soon after midnight one November night in 1871, as fog moved in, the schooner Merrow struck the shoal and three of her crew drowned before dawn.

Captain Danby, who had come down the coast on a fair wind, said he had taken Gannet's light for Kelby's harbor lamp and asked that the harbor lamp be painted red. The schooner's owners pressed for a new lens, calling the old one weak and its beam too dim to carry. The pilots of Kelby sent the board a petition: the Merrow's pilot, a stranger, had steered too close to the point, and every pilot working the channel ought to hold a license.

The inquiry found that the shoal had shifted since the charts were made, and it urged a lightship beside Tarrow. Holm had rung the bell all night, and Lise's logbook marks each stroke until dawn. He spent the week after the hearing on the rocks, striking a borrowed church bell into a heavy surf while Lise walked the beach marking where each stroke was drowned out.

The board had little money to spend, and a lightship would have consumed most of it. Its chairman, Amos Reddick, said that a man who had stood thirteen winters on the point knew its weather better than any inquiry, and on the keeper's account of the night the board ordered a heavier bell.

It went up in 1872, low on the rock where Lise's marks showed a stroke carried farthest. In the eighteen years Holm kept the light after that, nothing larger than a rowboat touched Tarrow in fog, and the bell still hangs where he placed it, struck by machine at his old rate of one stroke a minute.

For thirty-two years Ezra Holm kept the light on Gannet Point, the low headland guarding the channel into Kelby. Off the point lie the breakers of Tarrow Shoal; Kelby's harbor lamp burned two miles farther up, and on clear nights both lights were visible from the gallery. Captain Danby said he had taken Gannet's light for Kelby's harbor lamp and asked that the harbor lamp be painted red. The schooner's owners pressed for a heavier bell, insisting that the old one had been drowned out by the surf. The pilots of Kelby sent the board a petition: the Merrow's pilot, a stranger, had steered too close to the point, and every pilot working the channel ought to hold a license. The inquiry gave each party a fair hearing.

Then it found that the shoal had shifted since the charts were made, and it urged a lightship beside Tarrow. Holm had a different hour in mind. Lise's logbook shows that the lamp burned low before midnight, its old lens sooted and its beam weak, and that he climbed twice to trim it before the Merrow struck. He asked the clerk to read that entry aloud a second time.

The board had little money to spend, and the lightship would take most of it. It voted the money all the same, its chairman, Amos Reddick, saying that a board which called an inquiry must abide by what it found. The keeper's account of the night went into the minutes beside the vote.

Holm went on trimming the old lamp through every fog for seventeen more years, and each spring he wrote to the board asking for a new lens, in letters that grew shorter as his hand grew stiffer. The lens arrived in 1890, two months after he retired. Lise, keeper now, lit it and wrote to tell him how far it carried.

passage:
For thirty-two years Ezra Holm kept the light on Gannet Point, the low headland guarding the channel into Kelby. Off the point lie the breakers of Tarrow Shoal; Kelby's harbor lamp burned two miles farther up, and on clear nights both lights were visible from the gallery. In fog a bell was rung by hand for every vessel that passed inside the point, and his daughter Lise kept the logbook. Soon after midnight one November night in 1871, as fog moved in, the schooner Merrow struck the shoal and three of her crew drowned before dawn.

Captain Danby said he had taken Gannet's light for Kelby's harbor lamp and asked that the harbor lamp be painted red. The pilots of Kelby sent the board a petition blaming the bell, which the surf, they said, had drowned out, and asking for a heavier one. Holm answered with the logbook. Lise made a fair copy of it for the inquiry, and its entry for that night shows the Merrow passing close inside the point: the work, Holm said, of her pilot, a stranger who had steered too close and held no license.

The inquiry found that the shoal had shifted since the charts were made, and it urged a lightship beside Tarrow. The schooner's owners, who could recover their loss only if the light were at fault, pressed for something else: the old lens was weak, they argued, and its beam too dim. They wrote to every member of the board.

The board had little money to spend. Its chairman, Amos Reddick, whose brother held shares in the Merrow, moved that the Gannet lamp be fitted with a new lens, and the motion carried without debate. The keeper's account of the night was entered in the minutes and went no further.

Holm kept at it. For two years he wrote to the Kelby paper, naming the Merrow's pilot, Orrin Tay, in every letter; masters along the coast stopped taking Tay aboard, and he left the sea for an inland mill. Holm, whose light had come through the inquiry with a new lens and an unblemished record, wrote for a third year.

passage:
For thirty-two years Ezra Holm kept the light on Gannet Point, the low headland guarding the channel into Kelby. Off the point lie the breakers of Tarrow Shoal; Kelby's harbor lamp burned two miles farther up, and on clear nights both lights were visible from the gallery. In fog a bell was rung by hand for every vessel that passed inside the point, and his daughter Lise kept the logbook. Soon after midnight one November night in 1871, as fog moved in, the schooner Merrow struck the shoal and three of her crew drowned before dawn.

Captain Danby blamed his pilot, a stranger without a license who had steered too close to the point. The schooner's owners pressed for a new lens, calling the old one weak and its beam too dim to carry. The pilots of Kelby sent the board a petition asking for a heavier bell, since the old one, they said, had been drowned out by the surf. Holm called Lise, sixteen, her fair hair tucked under a sou'wester, to read the logbook's entry: both lights, Gannet's and Kelby's, visible from the gallery that night.

The inquiry found that the shoal had shifted since the charts were made, and it urged a lightship beside Tarrow. Holm offered a simpler story. A captain coming down in fog, he told the hearing, sees two lights and steers for the wrong one, having taken Gannet's light for Kelby's harbor lamp. The inquiry heard him out.

The board had little money to spend, and the estimates were read aloud: four hundred pounds for a lightship, ninety for a lens, eleven shillings for paint to turn Kelby's harbor lamp red. The keeper's account of the night was quoted in the minutes, but the vote followed the figures, and the harbor lamp was painted red that spring.

It was an explanation that asked nothing of the light Holm kept, and he gave it to every visitor for eighteen years. In 1894 a survey placed Tarrow Shoal three hundred yards seaward of the old charts. Two ships had struck it in the meantime, both on clear nights, with Kelby's red lamp in plain view.
